FOREWORD

This second volume contains the translation of the Vendidad, the Yashts, and the Khorda-Avesta, that is to say, it completes the full translation of the Avesta, minus the Fragments. The considerable size of the volume forces me to place the Fragments, the Errata, and the Index in a separate Appendix to appear shortly, to which I am adding several observations on the history of the literature and doctrines of Zoroastrianism.
The first volume gave the reader the liturgy of Zoroastrianism: this one gives the legislation and the epic, or rather the remnants of the legislation and the epic.

The new documentary sources are less abundant for the Vendidad than they were for the Yasna. For the text, I am limited to the editions of Westergaard and Spiegel, the corresponding portion of Geldner's edition not yet having appeared.
For the traditional aids, I draw first on those I had at my disposal for my English translation of 1880, — namely the Pahlavi text of London, the Persian translation of Munich, and the Gujarati translation of Frâmji ¹. The very thorough analysis of the Vendidad contained in the

These translations are very uneven: some represent an authentic tradition, not as ancient as the translations of the Vendidad and the Yasna, but one that has preserved their spirit. Such are the translations published in the Études iraniennes and those of the Khorda-Avesta in Pahlavi by Kanga. The others are relatively recent works made by Dasturs as much at a loss as ourselves: there has been a break in continuity. Such are in particular the translations of no. 5 and the Pahlavi translation of the Yasht of Bahrâm (see Yt. XIV). The agreement of this translation with the Persian translation of the manuscript of Dastur Darab proves that it is not

of unequal value. The texts for which one has no direct aid would be untranslatable, were it not that fortunately they deal with concrete subjects, whose language presents fewer of those technical mysteries so numerous in the Vendidad and the Yasna and which tradition alone can illuminate, and were it not that the body of Persian epic literature often provides a faithful paraphrase of them. To the rich information furnished by the Book of Kings of Firdausi and the Chronicles of Persian origin, the Grand Bundahish and the Pahlavi Shâh Nâmak add an abundant harvest of unpublished documents of which I have made extensive use.


yet it is not in the last few generations that these attempts have been made. That of Tir Andâz is the work of an intelligent man, who does not have tradition at his disposal everywhere, but who makes skillful use of what he does have and who possesses a feeling for the ancient language and literature.

INTRODUCTION

CHAPTER I

THE VENDIDAD

I. The Vendidad is one of the twenty-one Nasks that made up the Avesta in the time of the Sassanids. — The seven legal Nasks. — A summary analysis of the Vendidad. — The relationship of the Vendidad to the other legal Nasks. — Its religious importance as a code of purification.

II. Legal purity: an entirely physiological conception. — Impurity through death. — The Druj Nasu, demon of contagion. — Expulsion of the Nasu by the Sag-did. — Purification by the góméz. — The hygienic character of purification ceremonies. — Purity of the earth. — Purity of water. — Purity of fire. — The blending of hygienic conceptions with the theological and abstract conception of the purity of the elements. — Purification through death. — The impurity of a woman during her menstrual period; of a pregnant woman. — The impurity of material objects.

III. Civil law. Contracts. — Penal law. Assault and battery.

IV. Penalties. — Physical punishment. Flagellation. The Sraoshô-carana. — A table of penalties and offenses. — Conversion of physical punishment into a fine. — Moral punishment. Penance. — Inexpiable crimes. — To what extent the legislation of the Vendidad is real or ideal. — On procedure. The Ratu and the Sraoshàvarez.

I

The sacred literature of Zoroastrianism, in the era of the Sassanids, formed a whole divided into twenty-one books or Nasks¹, in remembrance of the twenty

1. The analysis of these Nasks is preserved for us in the eighth and ninth books of the Dinkart (translated by M. West in the fourth volume of his Pahlavi Texts).

VI ANNALS OF THE GUIMET MUSEUM

and a few words of the Ahuna Vairya. One of these Nasks has been preserved for us in its entirety ¹: it is the nineteenth ², the Vendidad.

The Vendidad has often been described as the book of the Laws of the Parsis, and we ourselves retain an analogous expression in the title of this volume: but it is only a conventional and approximate title that needs to be defined and explained.

The twenty-one Nasks of the Avesta had been distributed, more or less artificially, into three classes, each composed of seven Nasks. There were seven Nasks called gásánik or gáthic, comprising the Stót Yasht, which is found, mixed with extraneous material, in our Yasna, and around which the six other Nasks had developed and grouped themselves, commenting on, expanding, and completing that central text. Then came seven Nasks called dátik or legal, that is to say, dealing with civil, penal, and religious law. Finally came the Nasks called Hádak-mánsarik, which treated mixed subjects — historical, legendary, and scientific. The Vendidad is the representative of the legal Nasks, but it was not the only one. It is therefore not the Code of Zoroastrian law, but a section of that Code.

We possess in the Dinkart an analysis of the six other legal Nasks. Only four of them strictly merit that title: the Nikátûm, the Ganbásar-nijat, the Húspáram, and the Sakátûm. The first, second, and fourth dealt primarily with civil and penal law; the third, of which many fragments survive, dealt with liturgy. The Citradát and the Bakán Yasht treat, the one of history and the other of the cult of the various Izeds, and belong only conventionally within the framework of the legal Nasks. A large portion of the Bakân Yasht has survived: it constitutes our present-day Yashts (see the following chapter). If we now turn to an analysis of the Vendidad, we find that the most considerable part of it is made up of laws of purification — that is, laws aimed at driving the demon out of objects he has defiled: it is the book of the Law considered in particular-

1. The only one according to tradition, but not in reality, for the Yasna, as was seen in the first volume (Introd., p. LXXXVII), has incorporated the entire Stót Yasht.
2. The nineteenth in the order of the Dinkart (VIII, 1, 12). Later Rivâyats, placing the Stót Yasht at the head — where the Dinkart puts it at the end — assign the Vendidad the twentieth rank.

ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — INTRODUCTION VII

ment as "enemy of the Daêvas," dâtem vîdaêvô-dâtem. This epithet vîdaêvô-dâtem, which applies in a general way to the whole Law¹, insofar as it must struggle against the impure powers, has become the special name of our Nask, because it is the one most particularly concerned with this struggle of the Law against demons, even though this struggle does not occupy it entirely.

The Vendidad is composed of twenty-two chapters or Fargards, of which the first two and the last three belong rather to the definition of the hâdak-mânsarik Nasks, being of a legendary or mythical character. The first is an enumeration of the Iranian lands created by Ahura and of the plagues that Ahriman sets against the creation of each of them. The second Fargard, which likewise concerns the origins of history, recounts how Ahura offered in vain to Yima Khshaêta (Jamshîd) the task of bringing his religion to mankind, how Yima refused, but accepted instead to govern the earth, to expand it, and to banish from it sickness and death. The same Fargard also describes the Var, built by Yima on Ahura's orders, to serve as a shelter for the finest specimens of animal and plant life, which will repopulate the earth after the devastation of the winters sent at the end of time by Mahrkusha. The last three Fargards deal with the origins of medicine (Farg. XXI), the healing power of the Waters (Farg. XXI), and that of the holy Word (Farg. XXII). If the editors of the Vendidad had paid any attention to order and composition, they would have placed immediately after the second Fargard the one that now occupies the nineteenth position, which is dedicated to the mission of the man who will fulfill the role refused by Yima, namely Zoroaster. This Fargard describes Ahriman's futile efforts to destroy or seduce Zoroaster, and gives in summary form the revelation of Ahura to Zoroaster.

Sixteen chapters remain, the Fargards III-XVIII, devoted almost entirely to questions of law. The greater part, the Fargards V-XII,

1. Farg. V, 23; cf. note 43.
2. In Pahlavi Jût-div-dât or Jût-shédâ-dât; the modern name is an Indian corruption of vi-daêvô-dâtem, vi-div-dât. The equivalence of the long vowel and the nasalized vowel is one of the most frequent phenomena in Prakrit India, from the time of Asoka onward (cf. Senart, Inscriptions de Piyadasi, I, 16 ff.).

VIII ANNALS OF THE GUIMET MUSEUM

deals principally with the impurity that arises from death or contact with a corpse, and with the means employed to rid oneself of it. Fargards XVI, XVII, and part of the XVIIIth deal with sexual impurities and others. Fargards XIII and XIV, together with part of the XVth, deal with the dog — its dignity, its rights, its virtues, and the penalties inflicted upon its killer. Fargard III deals with the cult of the earth. Fargard IV deals with contracts and penal law. Among all these texts, very few exhibit a perfect unity: only the shortest ones display this quality (for example: Farg. X, on the number of times one must repeat the principal exorcism formulas; Farg. XI, on the exorcism formulas used to drive the demon from various defiled objects; Farg. XII, on the duration of mourning according to the various degrees of kinship; Farg. XVII, on the manner of cutting one's hair and nails). Most are interrupted by digressions and formed of fragments that repeat themselves more than once from one Fargard to another,¹ and that rarely follow one another in the most rational and clear order.

This disorder is not entirely due to the shortcomings of the oriental mind and to the haste with which the remnants of ancient literature were classified, for better or worse, at the time of codification: it was greatly encouraged by the very form of the Vendidad. The revelation is delivered by Ahura in a series of responses to an equal number of questions posed by Zoroaster, and since these questions are specific rather than general, the exposition breaks up into a considerable number of independent fragments, whose succession and interconnection were exposed to all the mishaps that threaten poorly linked army units.

A portion of the subjects treated in the Vendidad reappeared also in other Nasks. The fourth Fargard, which deals with contracts and assault and injury, is far from exhausting the subject, which was treated more thoroughly in the Nikâtûm. One of the sections of that Nask, the Patkâr-ratistân, dealt with judicial inquiries; another, the Zatamistân, with blows; a third, the Réshistân, with injuries; a fourth, the Hamémélistân, with proceedings in

1. V, 45-62 = VII, 60-72; XIII, 52-56 = VIII, 53-57; VIII, 35-72, cf. IX, 12-36.

ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — INTRODUCTION IX

in general¹. The seventh Fargard of the Vendidad has pointed details about the organization of medicine and physicians' fees: the Nask Hûspârâm treated the subject anew and completed the data of the Vendidad². The thirteenth Fargard was not the only text devoted to the glory of the dog: an entire section of the Nask of thieves³, the Ganbâ-sar-nijat⁴, was consecrated to it. It is the laws of purification that give the Vendidad its distinctive character, for not only do they fill the greater part of it, but the other Nasks deal with them only incidentally; and this is probably the reason why the Vendidad has been preserved for us, while of the four other legal Nasks only a few citations remain in Pahlavi literature. These laws gave the Vendidad a religious value that the other Nasks, more concerned with profane matters, did not possess to the same degree. The interests and necessities of practical life constantly recalled and sustained laws of a more profane character: the laws of purification were more liable to be neglected and forgotten. That is why their reading was inserted into the grand office. The grand office, in fact — the office of the Vendidad, as it is called — contains a recitation of the Vendidad, distributed for this purpose among nine sections, which are intercalated throughout the Yasna-Vispéred⁵.

T. II. b

x ANNALS OF THE MUSÉE GUIMET

II

In the table of contents the reader will find an analysis of the subjects treated in the Vendidad. It will not be without value to set out here the general principles that emerge from it.

"Purity is, after birth, the greatest good for man ¹": such is the principle that dominates the Vendidad. This word for purity, yaozhdâo, although a moral idea or moral impression is associated with it, is nonetheless above all — at least in the Vendidad — a purely physical conception, and the word "cleanliness" would be more exact, if it had taken on the moral overtone that the Zend expression carries and that the English word cleanliness, for example, carries. The axiom Cleanliness is next to Godliness would be entirely Zoroastrian, with the difference that in Zoroastrianism Cleanliness is itself a form of Godliness.

Legal impurity always has physiological causes. The impure object par excellence is the corpse: also impure is everything that leaves the human body, whether natural secretions or parts separated artificially, such as hair and nails. But to speak of impurity is to speak of contagion: for the corpse breeds corruption and plague; the impurities of the living body breed disease; hair breeds vermin ². The purpose of purification is to drive out this contagion that passes from the dead to the living, from the living to the living, and the theory of impurity and of

Vd. XIX-XX: after Ys. LIII, Vp. XXIII; that is, immediately after the Gâtha Vahishtoishti.
Vd. XXI-XXII: after Ys. LIV, Vp. XXIV; that is, immediately after the Airyama ishyô.
In other words, the Vendidad is inserted into the Gâthas at the natural subdivisions formed by the divisions of the Gâthas themselves.
In place of the Vendidad, the Vishtâsp Yasht is sometimes inserted, which is an abridged Vendidad: the office then takes the title of Vishtâsp Sadé (see p. 664). There are only eight sections instead of nine: the point of insertion is the same as for the first eight of the Vendidad.
1. Yasna XLVIII, 5 c; cited Vd. V, 21; X, 18.
2. Cf. Vd. XVII, 3.

ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — INTRODUCTION XI

purification would in fact reduce to a theory of hygiene, were it not that this contagion is conceived as the work of supernatural beings, that our microbes are elevated into Daêvas, and that certain theological conceptions, joined by certain popular superstitions, come to obscure and hinder the development of a medicine that is half experimental and half infantile.

At the moment when life leaves the body — if the death is natural, at the next Gâh; if the death is violent, immediately — a demon takes possession of the corpse; this is the Druj of the cadaver, the Druj Nasu¹: she swoops down from the region of hell in the form of a horrible fly — the fly of corpses. To drive her away, or at least to weaken her power, a white dog with yellow ears, or a dog with four eyes (that is, with two spots above the eyes)², is brought before the dead man: at the moment it brings its muzzle close to the corpse, the Druj flees. This is what is called the Sag-did, "the look of the dog." It was perhaps thought that the dog, which sees death coming and howls at death, has insights and powers over it that man does not possess. The more extraordinary and rare the animal's appearance, the greater the degree to which it was thought to possess these protective virtues. In practice, however, less was demanded regarding the dog's appearance: the Sag-did could be performed by a shepherd's dog, a house dog, a stray dog (Vohunazga), or a dog trained for hunting (Tauruna); failing these, by birds of prey — the mountain falcon, the raven, the eagle³. When the shadow of the bird passed over the dead man, the Nasu was struck⁴.

The Sag-did does not, however, suffice to destroy the Nasu, and the man who touches the dead body is nonetheless seized by the contagion and affected, either by direct pollution (ham-raêthwa) or by indirect pollution (paiti-raêthwa). If the Sag-did has taken place over the body, the impurity being less severe, it will suffice for the person to purify himself by washing with góméz (that is, with ox urine) and with water⁵. If the Sag-did has not taken place, he

XII ANNALES DU MUSÉE GUIMET

will have to undergo, three times, at intervals of three days, a long and painful series of purifications¹ with gômêz, and then with water, accompanied by a Sag-did performed by a living person. The Sag-did of the living is necessary because, since the one for the dead was not performed, the Druj Nasu has passed from the dead to the living in full force. As for the use of gômêz, it belongs to folk medicine: it was considered the disinfectant par excellence, and still is, not only in Persia but in India itself, where it serves as a remedy against leprosy, as it reportedly did for the very first time in the case of King Jamshîd³. For as long as the purification lasts, the impure person remains isolated from the faithful whom he would defile, in a kind of lazaretto called the arméshtgâh, "the place of the infirm, of the immobile."

We describe further on⁴ the funeral ceremonies: it will be seen that they can be summed up in two words — two words of the hygienist: isolate the center of infection, destroy that center. What distinguishes the Zoroastrian conception from the European one is that we concern ourselves with isolating and destroying the dead element only in cases of so-called infectious disease: in Zoroastrianism, death is always infectious and contagious. We leave it to the earth to take care of destroying the germs of corruption: in Zoroastrianism, to do so is to defile the earth and poison it. When a corpse is buried, the Genius of the earth, Spenta-Ârmaiti, shudders⁵. For one year it is forbidden to till the ground on which a corpse has rested⁶. The ground in which a corpse has been buried is impure for fifty years (the time necessary for the corpse to be destroyed)⁷. Hence also all those measures that follow upon death; the precautions taken to isolate the body not only from people but from the earth itself, by placing it on an insulating layer of sand or an impermeable stone slab⁸; hence those fumigations of perfumes that destroy the demon in all the

ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — INTRODUCTION XIII

in whichever directions the wind carries them¹; hence the transfer of the body to remote and barren heights² or to the summit of specially constructed towers, the Dakhmas³. Wild beasts and birds of prey quickly strip the corpse of its fatty parts, which are the principal seat of corruption and infection⁴.

It is the fluid element, indeed, that is the seat and chief conductor of impurity. It is through water, modern thinkers would say, that microbes are transmitted: "the dry does not mingle with the dry," says the Vendidad. Hence also the harmlessness of a corpse after the lapse of one year⁶; and hence finally the prohibition against throwing corpses into water, a crime punishable by death⁷.

It is fire that among us is the great purifier. Zoroastrianism, abandoning here the experimental and utilitarian ground in favor of theological theory, applies to fire the same laws as to earth and water. Lost in contemplation of the flame of the sacred fire, it sees nothing beyond the fact that fire purifies all things, and watches over its purity with anxiety. To burn a corpse is a capital crime⁸. The ideal would be for fire to burn eternally upon the altar, fed by the priest with dry and fragrant wood, and doing battle against invisible demons. The necessities of life degrade it to all manner of profane uses: religion at least intervenes to restore it to its original purity through a series of operations that are for fire what the Barashnûm is for man⁹.

This is not the only case where naturalistic experience yields to the mystical principle. Death defiles only when it overtakes one of Ormazd's creatures: the corpse of a creature of Ahriman — whether human, namely an idolater, a heretic, or a harmful beast — does not defile the one who

XIV ANNALS OF THE MUSÉE GUIMET

This is because the wicked man, as long as he lives, harbors the Druj within himself: when he dies, she carries his soul off to hell and the body becomes pure. When it is a righteous man, it is the Druj who comes from hell to seize the body that was pure during his lifetime. The theorists of Mazdaism doubtless did not go so far as to demonstrate that the corpse of an impious man is exempt from corruption, or to permit his burial: but those who came into contact with such a corpse were freed from the ceremonies of purification.

After death, the most frequent and most formidable source of impurity is that of a woman during her menstrual period — the dashtán woman. Throughout her period of impurity, she is kept apart, in an isolated room on the ground floor, in the armêsht-gâh (p. XII), called for this occasion the dashtánishtan; her food is given to her at a distance on a spoon fixed to a pole. Even her gaze is impure and would defile the fire². One will find in PLINY³ and in Leviticus⁴ commentary on or parallels to these Mazdean conceptions and customs.

A pregnant woman near her time of delivery is treated as a dashtán. Childbirth is a legally impure act, and for forty days after delivery she remains isolated in the arméht-gâh, and whoever touches her becomes impure. At the end of forty days she may leave her confinement, undergoes the Barashnûm, and returns to common life, which is interrupted in this way every month⁵. These practices, often deadly, today challenged by Parsi opinion⁶, but not yet abolished, rest, according to

ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD — INTRODUCTION xv

defenders, based on a protective idea that aims to ensure absolute rest for the sick woman at the moment when she most needs it. The true cause seems to be that she is in danger of death: for when a person dies, there is a danger that death will linger in the house ¹.

Everything that comes out of a human being is impure, even the air one exhales. Hence the use of a veil over the nose and mouth, the Paitidâna, worn by the priest before the fire and while eating ². Hence also the ceremonies that accompany the cutting of hair and nails and the formulas that neutralize their dangers ³.

Objects are naturally susceptible to impurity just as persons are. They resist it more or less, depending on whether the material of which they are made is more or less penetrable or porous, and the duration of purification varies inversely. Metal vessels can be purified; earthen vessels, once defiled, cannot be purified and are taken out of use. The power of resistance to impurity fortunately follows the relative value of materials: gold, silver, iron, steel, stone, earth, wood, clay ⁴. Leather is purified more easily than cloth ⁵; dry wood more easily than green wood ⁶. Purification procedures will also differ according to the season, being more summary during summer, the dry season, than during winter, the wet season.


III

Properly speaking, law occupies only one Fargard, the fourth, dealing with contracts and assaults against the person, and some portions of the thirteenth, dealing with quasi-offenses.
Contracts (mithrô) are classified according to their object, which is either a

In the section on blows and injuries, the Vendidad recognizes seven degrees: the âgerepta, or the act of seizing a weapon to strike; the avaoirishta, or the act of brandishing the weapon to strike; the aredush, or the simple blow; the blow that bruises; the blow that draws blood; the blow that breaks a bone; and the mortal wound⁴. The gravity of an unexpiated offense⁵ — that is, one not redeemed by punishment and penance — increases with each repetition and rises at each recurrence to the level of the offense immediately above it. Thus the âgerepta, committed seven times in succession, without any full expiation having interrupted the progression and restored the sinner to a state of innocence, is equivalent to homicide⁶.

IV

For every crime there is a penalty in this world and one in the next. The punishment in the next world is only suffered if the crime has not been expiated on earth. Let us therefore speak of expiation on earth.

Expiation on earth consists of two elements: a material element and a moral element; in other words: a physical punishment and penance.

The physical punishment generally consists of a certain number of strokes with an instrument called the Aspahê ashtra or the Sraoshô-carana: the first term literally means "instrument for urging the horse," the second means "instrument that produces obedience": it is doubtless a matter of the whip and leather thongs ¹.

The unit for the highest penalties is 200 strokes of the Sraoshô-carana, and the guilty party who has merited this punishment is called peshotanu. The word seems to literally mean "one who pays with his body²": but it has lost its original sense, and in legal passages it is always used when the penalty in question is 200 strokes³: it is never used when the penalty

These are quite extravagant figures, and they prove that these formulas should not all be taken literally and need to be interpreted. A fragment of the Avesta gives us a glimpse of how. It is known that at the passage into the other world, the deeds of the dead are weighed in the balance of Rashnu¹ and that this weighing decides their fate. Now it is said² that the soul goes to Paradise or Hell depending on whether good deeds outweigh evil ones, or vice versa, by three Srôshcaranâm: if they are in balance, to within three Srôshcaranâm, the soul goes to Hamêstagân, or Purgatory. To speak of weight is to speak of value, and the commentaries indeed inform us that a Tanâfûhr — that is, the 200 strokes of Sraoshô-carana which the Peshôtanu must endure — is worth 300 istirs, or, since an istir equals 4 dirhems³, 1,200 dirhems; in other words, 300 staters or 1,200 drachmas⁴. Ten thousand strokes of Srôshcaranâm amount to 50 Tanâfûhrs, that is to say, 60,000 drachmas.

Expiation does not always consist entirely of lashes. In a certain number of cases — for the killing of the water-dog, for example, or for commerce with a dashtân woman — expiation also involves the performance of a certain number of good works. These good works are: the offering of sacrifice; the killing of harmful animals, of Ahrimanian animals; gifts to priests, warriors, and farmers of all the tools of their trade; acts of charity toward the poor; care given to animals; and the construction of works of public utility ².

Moral expiation proper — the purification of the soul — consists in repentance, that is to say, in the recitation of the Patet, or formula of repentance, accompanied by a resolution to sin no more. This is the idea sometimes expressed by saying that the Mazdean Religion (spayêiti) expels from the guilty the greatest crimes he may have committed ³.

Moral expiation takes effect above all in the next world: it frees from the punishments of hell, because it cancels the fault. But it does not free from penalties in this world: thus the bearer who has carried a corpse alone, the incompetent priest who has undertaken a purification he is incapable of performing, are punished by death — but penitence saves their soul ⁴.

There are a certain number of crimes that are anâperetha, inexpiable; ayaozhdya, unpurifiable; that is to say, they are punished by death here below and there is no salvation for the soul, not even through repentance. Such is the crime of one who burns a corpse, who eats carrion, who commits the sin against nature. The sodomite, the burner of corpses, the highway robber, caught in the act, may be killed by any passer-by, without a judge's ruling ⁵. But a certain number of sins are called anâperetha purely by metaphor, to emphasize their enormity, for repentance redeems them. Such is the case of the man who buries a corpse without digging it up before the end of the second year (III, 38-42; cf. I, 13), or who defiles himself (VIII, 27-30).

But a series of foreign documents proves to us that in fact a large part of the laws of the Vendidad were actually applied: we know from Strabo that the pollution of fire and water was indeed punishable by death (Farg. VIII, note 70); we see in Procopius (I, 11) a chief minister, Seoses, put to death for having buried his wife. It is quite true that in certain prescriptions which astonish us, and which seem to us hardly practicable, one is tempted to see a simple device of edification. The disproportionate penalties inflicted in certain cases would have had the purpose of highlighting certain views of practical utility, such as respect for useful animals, or certain views of hygienic morality that simple counsel or moderate penalties would have insufficiently protected against ignorance, negligence, or brutality. But it is always difficult to say, in matters of religious legislation, where fact ends and theory begins: the example of certain periods of our Middle Ages proves to us that, with circumstances and secular power lending their aid, religious theory can go in practice much further than one would ever have imagined. Thus, confining ourselves to the Sassanid period, the only one in which Zoroastrianism was the state religion and in which the Avesta could have had the force of strict law, I do not believe that all the articles of the Mazdean Code were or could have been applied by judges: but, when the occasion arose, they could be invoked and could provide the basis for persecutions and harassment which, as the example of Seoses proves, could go even beyond the written text, since no known text punishes with death the burial of bodies. Thus the theory furnished fanaticism with an arsenal of weapons that generally lay dormant, no doubt, within the precincts of the temple or the school, but which, under a clerical prince, could easily emerge from the shadows and strike deadly blows.

I

The word yasht, Zend yêshti, does not differ in its literal meaning from yasna: it is worship, the cult, just as yasna is. But, applied to the special cult of the various Izeds, it came to designate the texts whose recitation is the essential element of that cult; and the words "Yasht of Bahrâm," for example, after having designated the cult rendered to Bahrâm, came to designate the text recited in honor of Bahrâm.
Each of the thirty days of the month, as is well known, is under the control of a certain Ized, whose name it bears and whose name is invoked each day in a special formula. The collection of these thirty formulas forms the Siróza, which is sometimes recited all together, in honor not of the thirty days of the month, but of the thirty principal divinities¹.

II

The great interest of the Yashts lies in the large number of details
they provide on mythology and in particular on the epic tradition of Persia.
Five of these Yashts in particular — the Yashts of Abân, Gosh, Râm, Ard,
and Zamyâd — show us the great heroes of legend offering sacrifice
to the various Izeds and imploring their aid¹ in occasions where they
are in need of supernatural assistance. They thus give us, each complementing
the other, the framework of the legendary history of Iran, past and future, from
Haoshyanha, the first king, down to Vishtâspa, the champion of the new
religion, and down to Saoshyañt, the Savior of the last times.
The examination of the heroic legends described or assumed by the Yashts
and the order in which the heroes succeed one another in the invocations leads
to an important conclusion: not only is there a perfect agreement
in substance between the heroic legend of the Avesta and that found
in the epic literature of the Persian period — that is, in the Book
of Kings and the Chronicles — but the succession and chronology itself
had already been fixed and established in an absolutely precise manner. For example,
the Zamyâd Yasht, in tracing the history of the transmission of the Hvarenô, or
Royal Glory, from Ahura down to Saoshyañt, gives us a succession
of dynasties that is exactly that of Firdausi. It is partly

The period, so abbreviated and so incoherent in Firdausi, which follows the reign of Minûcihr, was therefore treated in the Avesta in a definite and systematic manner. Not only are the successions the same, but even the lengths of reigns appear already fixed. Takhma Urupa already reigns for thirty years, as in the later chronology. The epic fragments of the Avesta thus belong to a systematic whole, already worked out in all its details and settled in its overall shape. Each heroic figure is already everything it will become, and it arrives already in its own time and at its own hour. Here are the broad outlines of this history according to the Zamyâd Yasht²:

The Yashts do not merely provide the framework of the royal epic: they reveal its vast gaps and sometimes fill them in. That passage of the Zamyâd Yasht (§93) which shows Franhrasyan carrying the Hvarenô while he kills Zainigao, illuminated by a passage in Firdausi showing the Arabs invading Iran during the absence of Kai Kâûs and being driven back by Afrâsyâb, singularly broadens the field of epic legend and introduces into it all manner of international complications. The legend of Husravah is richer in the Yashts by an entire cycle of heroic tales than in Firdausi: the cycle of Aurvasâra, with its battles and its rides through the White Forest. The cycle of Naotara, which has left only a proper name in the Persian epic, is still rich in enigmatic and dramatic details¹. Of the wondrous wars of Vishtâspa against the enemies of Zoroastrianism, the names of Arejaṭ-aspa and Vañdaremaini, his brother, are the only ones that survive on the Turanian side in the Shah Nameh: what has become of Ashta-aurvañt, son of Vîspô-thaurvô-asti, and of Peshana, Spinjaurusha, Darshinika, worshippers of the Daêvas; and of Tâthravañt, of the evil religion, Peshô-canha, burier of corpses²?

CHAPTER III

THE KHORDA-AVESTA

The Khorda-Avesta or Small Avesta generally designates the collection of prayers recited by the faithful in the ordinary circumstances of life, as opposed to the liturgical texts recited by the priest. A number of manuscripts, followed sometimes by European editions and translations, include within it the Yashts and the Sirozas — in other words, include under this title everything that remains of the Avesta once the three books of the great liturgy are deducted: the Yasna, the Vispered, and the Vendidad. The absence of ancient manuscripts and the absence of the name in ancient Pahlavi literature make it impossible to trace the history of the name or to determine exactly the collection to which it applied¹. Since the Yashts — at least sixteen of them — form a defined whole of ancient origin, I have thought it worthwhile to give them a separate and independent place, and I have had them preceded by the Siroza for reasons of clarity and because of the exact correspondence between the two orders of texts. The Siroza, moreover, is generally not included in the small editions, whether manuscript or printed, of the Khorda-Avesta: it belongs to

A modern tradition attributes the formation of the Khorda-Avesta to Adarbâd Mahraspand, the last editor of the Avesta under Sapor II² (309-379). This tradition, which cannot be traced in any text known to me, contains at least an element of ideal truth, if the name of Adarbâd symbolizes the work of definitive classification of sacred literature and the liturgy.

The elements of the Khorda-Avesta itself have little originality. I find in the analysis of the Nasks no text whose definition it corresponds to, and the greater part of the elements of which it is composed can be found either in the Yasna or in the Yashts. The Fargard that opens the Vendidad contains, to use the terms of the Dînkart (VIII, 42,2), "the enumeration of sixteen excellent countries created [by Auhrmazd] and of the plagues corresponding to each of them, [sent by Ahriman]"¹. Indeed, for each new country created by Ahura, Añgra Mainyu responds by creating a plague, of a physical or moral order, designed to corrupt the native perfection of the divine creation: this counter-creation is called paityâra, literally "reaction, obstacle."

These sixteen regions all belong to Iran. Attempts were once made to draw far-reaching historical conclusions from the order in which they are arranged, which was thought to retrace the progress of Iranian colonization descending from the plateau of Central Asia². The enumeration offers natural series that seem to indicate a certain systematic order: nos. 2–7 — Sogdiana, Margiana, Bactria, Nisâya between Merv and Bactres, Herat, Caboul — form a compact group covering the northeast, the far Khorasan. Nos. 8–9 — Urva-Mésène and Gurgân — connect by a line to the west the two seas, the Persian Gulf and the Caspian Sea; nos. 10–11 bring us back to the east (Arachosia and Seistan); nos. 12 and 14 bring us back to the northwest with Rai and Tabaristan: if no. 13, Cakhra, is in the same region, we will have a massive and continuous northern group; if it is the Carkh of the country of Ghaznin (note 36), it will again be the same back-and-forth from west to east; no. 15 with the Indus, no. 16 with the Ranha, that is to say with the Tigris, give us

XX, 32) and founds his religion (Bd. XXXII, 3); it is there that the first animal couple appears (Bd. XIV, 4 and Zád Spa-ram, IX, 8). Judging by its name, it was also no doubt the cradle of the Iranians, for this name literally means "Iranian Seed," or what comes to the same thing, "Seed of the Aryas" (airyana being the adjective derived from arya, airya). But where is Irâ Vêj? It is generally agreed to look for it to the east, on the side of the Oxus, and there are two plausible reasons for this: the first is that the lands that follow in the enumeration lie to the east of Iran (Sogdiana, Margiana, Bactria); the second is that during the Sassanid period the word vaṅuhi, which forms part of the name of the river of Irân Vêj, became, in its Pahlavi form Vêh, the name of the Oxus: it designates the Oxus in the Bundahish (XX, 22, 28), among the Armenian writers, and among the Chinese pilgrims (Garrez, Journal asiatique, 1869, II, 169-198). But against these inferences — of which only the second carries real weight, since the order of succession changes several times (see the Introduction to the Fargard) — positive testimonies arise which compel us to seek Irân Vêj at the other end of Iran, to the west. According to the Bundahish, "Irân Vêj is beside Âdarbaijân" (Airán-vêj pun kóstaki Âtûrpâ-tagán; XXIX, 12). Since Âdarbaijân is bounded to the east by the Caspian and to the west by the regions of the Raṅha (see § 20), the neighboring region that the Bundahish has in view can only be Media proper, which lies to the south, or the Karabagh, which lies to the north. Media being, for the Magi, the heart of Iran, the designation of Airyanem Vaêjo would suit it perfectly, were it not that the climatic indications point us northward: for at the latitude of Media the prolonged winters of the Airyanem Vaêjô are unknown. Spiegel has already connected the Airyanem Vaêjô with Arràn (Eranische Alterthumskunde, I, 194, 212), and while this form Arrân is not entirely above reproach from a phonetic standpoint — the normal representative of Airyana being Erân — it presents no insurmountable difficulty, for the assimilation of Ary to Arr may be a purely dialectal feature peculiar to the region. Stephanus of Byzantium cites a region Ἀριανία, bordering the land of the Cadusians (Ἀριανία ἔθνος προσεχὲς τοῖς Καδουσίοις; Spiegel, ibid., p. 212): the Cadusians belonged to Gilan, and Ἀριανία may well designate the Arrân.

The beauty and fertility of Karabagh, "the black garden," are celebrated throughout the Caucasus: but its winter is among the longest and most rigorous. At Nôrûz, as a native of Karabagh, Ahmed Bey Agaeff, informs us, the fields are still under snow: the temperature does not begin to moderate until around April 15-20, and flowering does not begin until the first days of May. Summer, marked by the migration of nomads from the plain to the mountains, begins around June 20 and ends around mid-August: that is to say, if by summer one means the period of great heat that makes the plain uninhabitable, it lasts barely two months, just like the summer of Irân Vêj (§ 4).

If Iran Vêj is the Arrân, then Karabagh, the Vañuhi Dâitya will be the Aras, the ancient Araxes. The distinguishing feature of the Dâitya is that it is infested with reptiles (see § 3), which is likewise one of the distinctive traits of the Araxes: see note 5. The fact that the name Vañuhi is applied to the Oxus under the Sassanids does not prove that the Vañuhi Dâitya is not the Araxes: it is possible that the two rivers facing each other on either side of the Caspian were regarded as one and the same river — just as under the Sassanids the Indus and the Oxus were considered one and the same river (Garrez, l. l., 195); the main branch was called Vañuhi (âp), "the Good River"; the smaller branch, sanctified by the birth of Zoroastrianism, will have been called "the Vañuhi of the Law," which is the meaning of Vañuhi Dâitya.

XX, 19), as well as among Arab geographers, who designate by سغد the river and valley of the Zarafshan. The most celebrated part of this valley was called the Soghd of Samarkand and was considered one of the four most beautiful sites in the world. Along a valley of eight days' march, it was said to be nothing but "an uninterrupted tangle of greenery and gardens. These gardens are surrounded by inexhaustible rivers; beyond the gardens, on each side, there are cultivated fields, and beyond these fields pastures for livestock. It is of all the lands that God has given to man the most agreeable and the one where the trees are most beautiful" (Geography of Abulfeda, tr. Guyard, II, 213). The Pahlavi translation transports or seems to transport Sughdha to the banks of the Euphrates: it reads: gavâi Sûrik mânishn, ât dashti Sûrik mânishn "the plain of Syria"; which the Grand Bundahishn interprets as Bagdâd: "the second [land] excellent that I created was the plain inhabited by the Sûrig, that is to say Bakdâd (created by the Gods: datigar pahlûm yahbûnt dashti Sûrig mânishn, aîghash Sûrig patash katarûnand: ît Bakdât, bagán-dât). Were it not for the persistence of the name Soghd, one would be tempted to see in Sûr-ik a phonetic deformation of Sughdha, and the origin of Sir in the name of the great Sogdian river, the Sir Darya: the assimilation to Bagdâd is evidently a scribal interpolation, born of a confusion between the land of Sûrik and Sûristân.

FARGARD 2

This Fargard is devoted to two legends concerning Yima Khshaêta (Jamshid), the great hero of Iranian prehistory, the founder of Persian civilization, the ideal of all power and all splendor.

In the first part (§§ 1-20), Ahura offers Yima the opportunity to receive his religion and communicate it to mankind: Yima declines, but agrees to take charge of the governance of the world, to make it prosper, and to drive away from it sickness and death. He receives the golden ring and the sword, symbols of sovereignty, and three times enlarges the earth by a third, as it has become too narrow for its inhabitants.

In the second part (§§ 21-43), Ahura announces to Yima the approach of a terrible winter that will destroy all life on earth: he commands him to build a Var in which he will gather the most perfect specimens of the human race and of all animal and plant species. Yima builds this Var, and within it men live the most blessed of existences.

The first legend belongs to the heroic and royal cycle. In the legendary history of Iran, as found in the Avesta³, Yima Khshaêta, son of Vîvanhat, is the third universal sovereign⁴: he reigns for a thousand years, during which neither sickness nor death appears on earth, and men live the life of Paradise⁵. But he lets himself be blinded by pride; the divine glory, the Hvarenô, abandons him⁶; he is overthrown from his throne and sawn in two by the three-headed Serpent, Azhi Dahâka (Zôhâk)⁷, who will in turn depopulate the earth for a thousand years, until Thaêtaona delivers the earth and chains him to Damâvand⁸.

According to the chronology of the Bundahish (XXXIV, 4), Yima, instead of filling an entire millennium, occupies only 616 years and 6 months, or more precisely 716 years and 6 months; for he reigns 616 years and 6 months and remains in hiding for 100 years⁹: the remainder of the millennium is filled by his predecessors, beginning with the first man, Gayomart¹⁰. In the Vedas, Yima, son of Vîvanhat, appears under the name of Yama, son of Vivasvat, as the first man and the first to die, and as the founder of the institution of worship. It is quite plausible that the millennium attributed to Yima is the memory of an older conception in which he was also the first representative of primitive humanity; and it was when Zoroastrianism conceived the abstract and symbolic figures of Gayomart, Mashya, and Mashyana that Yima yielded first place to these newcomers and surrendered to them part of his hazâr. His refusal to accept the role of apostle is the abdication in favor of Zoroaster of a role he had formerly fulfilled as

In our Fargard he is still the millennial sovereign: for he is seen to reign over three periods of three hundred years (§§ 8, 12, 16), and nothing suggests that his reign ends with the third period.

In the later chronology, Yim reigns only 616 years and 6 months: but he lives yet another century, hidden (pun nihânih): according to the Shâh Nâma, he hid from Zôhâk, but this cannot be the ancient version, for Zôhâk reigns a millennium, and if it was Zôhâk who drove Yim to flee, Zôhâk would have reigned 1,100 years. It therefore becomes very plausible that the last century of Yim was filled, not by the adventures of exile, but by the work whose account follows in our Fargard the history of his first nine centuries, and which is precisely a work accomplished "in a hidden place" (pun nuhaftakih, v. i., note 12), that is to say, by the construction of the underground Var. And indeed the Grand Bundahish, instead of the words "he was a hundred years in hiding," has the words: "after that he was a hundred years in the Var" (100 shant dar varik yahvûnt). The Var was not built as a refuge against Zôhâk, but as a refuge against the calamities of the end of the world; and that is the subject of the second legend.

The life of the world, according to Zoroastrianism, lasts a period of 12,000 years, divided into twelve millenniums or hazârs. The world lived in purely spiritual form for 3,000 years; in material form, but without mixture with the operations of Ahriman, for 3,000 years; from the invasion of Ahriman, three hazârs have elapsed, one ending at the death of Jamshid, the second at the death of Zôhâk, the third at the revelation of Zoroaster. At each of the three hazârs yet to run, one of the three sons of Zoroaster not yet born must appear: Oshêdar (Ukhshyaṭ-ereta), Oshêdar-mâh (Ukhshyaṭ-nemô), and Sôshyans (Saoshyañt)¹¹. Each of them appears at a moment when evil triumphs: he comes to restore the law and suppress the overflow of evil. The last, Sôshyans, comes after the unleashing of Zôhâk, who has broken his chain on the Damâvand: Zôhâk is definitively crushed by Sâm Keresâsp and Sôshyans appears

FARGARD 3

The Guebres, says Chardin (ed. Langlès, VIII, 358), "regard agriculture not only as a fine and innocent profession, but also as meritorious and noble, and they believe it is the foremost of all vocations, the one for which the sovereign God and the lesser gods, as they say, have the greatest pleasure and which they reward most generously. This belief, having become an article of faith among them, leads them naturally to work the land and to devote themselves to it above all else: their priests teach them that the most virtuous act is to beget children (cf. Farg. IV, 47 and notes) and after that to cultivate land that would otherwise lie fallow (cf. infra, § 4), to plant a tree, whether fruit-bearing or otherwise."

To the classical testimonies on the subject (Xenophon, Oeconomicus, IV, 4 ff.; Polybius, X, 28, cited in note 10, etc.) has been added a striking piece of evidence, recently discovered by MM. Cousin and Deschamps at Deremendjik, near Magnesia on the Maeander, which comes from Darius himself: it is a letter from the Great King to the satrap of Asia Minor, Gadates, congratulating him for having worked the king's land well and for having acclimatized in lower Asia the fruits from beyond the Euphrates (because you cultivate my land, transplanting to the lower regions of Asia the fruits from beyond the Euphrates, Bulletin de Correspondance hellénique, XIII, 529).

Fargard III is the commentary on these texts. The principal subject is, in the terms of the Dinkart,

The Achaemenids granted usufruct of land for five generations to laborers who brought water to places that previously had none (τοῖς ἐπί τινας τόπους τῶν μὴ πρότερον ἀρδευομένων ἐπεισαγομένοις ὕδωρ πηγαῖον: — Polybius, X, 28). From this arose a magnificent system of canals that sought out underground water near mountain ranges and circulated it throughout the whole expanse of Iran, the driest and most arid country in existence. Antiochus the Great, crossing the Parthian desert in pursuit of Arsaces, found underground water stored up by the subjects of the Achaemenids (Polybius, ibid.). Even today Persia survives only because of these underground canals or kanâts, the only public works she maintains at all, without which she would perish from hunger (cf. FARGARD 4

This Fargard is the only one in the Vendidad that belongs to legislation properly so called: it deals with contracts and assaults upon persons.

I a. Classification of contracts according to the value of their object (2); rescission of a contract by payment of the value of the immediately superior contract (3).

I b. Religious responsibility of the family for the violation of a contract by one of its members (4-11).

I c. Punishment of the Mihir-Druj, the one who violates a contract (12-16).

II a. Definition of assaults upon persons called âgerepta (threat), avaoirishta (attack), aredush (blow. — § 17).

II b. Punishment for the threat (18-21), for the attack (22-25), for the blow (26-29); for the blow that wounds (30-33); for the blow that draws blood (34-36); for the blow that breaks a bone (37-39); for the blow that kills (40-43).

III a. The duty of charity toward fellow believers: giving them money, a wife, instruction (44-45).

I d. The gravity of false oath in judicial trial (46).

III b. The dignity of wealth, marriage, and material life (47-49 a).

I d'. The judicial trial: the gravity of false oath (49 b-55).

9. The translation of this entire paragraph is conjectural: the difficulty lies in the meaning of the two technical expressions framarezaiti and añtare urvaitya fradathaiti. The first, translated fráj mâlêt, appears in Farg. III, 42, referring to the action of the wind sweeping away straw: it literally means "to remove by rubbing" and figuratively "to cancel, annul": thus it is said in the Avesta, vispem tat paiti framerezaiti dushmatemca, "it wipes away all evil thoughts" (Vd. Pahlavi, ad Westergaard VII, 54). The Pahlavi Commentary appends it to each of the five formulas where it appears with the name of the immediately lower contract, which leads to the meaning that a contract is canceled by the immediately superior contract, that is to say, in order to free oneself from the first one must deliver the value of the second; this is what the second expression conveys: "he delivers [such and such a value] according to agreement(?)". The case envisaged is not the one where a contract is violated, where one is mihirdruj, but the one where a person wishes to go back on a contract, to rescind it.

11. adha-cithanâm narâm nabànazdish tanâm. The patriarchal family system, in use in Zoroastrian Persia, quite naturally entailed collective family responsibility (cf. Dinkart, VIII, 20, 9): it extended even to criminal matters (Ammianus Marcellinus, XXIII, 6: Leges apud eos impendio formidatae, et abominatae aliae, per quas ob noxam unius omnis propinquitas perit).

12. satâish: tradition supplies the idea of years: 300 shant bim dârishn "they have to fear for three hundred years"; that is to say, according to Frâmji, that his relatives will have to perform the Patet for his soul for three hundred years. This would therefore be a religious responsibility, and not a civil one — the latter went without saying and presumably needed no explicit statement. Legal casuistry seems to have sought to reduce the circle of responsibility: "the son born after the sin alone has cause to fear; virtuous parents have nothing to fear; when the father dies, the virtuous son has nothing to fear." The Rivâyats transfer the entire punishment onto the guilty party and teach that he will be in hell for three hundred years.

FARGARD 5

This Fargard and the following ones, up to and including the twelfth, deal in particular with the impurity contracted through contact with a dead person, and with the means of restoring a person or object that has been defiled to a state of purity.

I (1-7). If a man involuntarily defiles fire (I a, 1-4) or water (I b, 5-7) by unknowingly bringing dead matter (nasu) into contact with them, he does not enter into a state of sin.

II (8-9). The innocence of fire (II a, 8) and water (II b, 9), which sometimes seem to kill, but do not actually kill.

III a (10-14). How to dispose of the bodies of the dead in winter, when it is impossible to carry them to the Dakhma.
III b (15-20). Why Ahura, who forbids man to defile water, causes rain to fall from the sky upon the Dakhmas laden with corpses, in order to purify them.
III c (21-26). The excellence of purity and the supreme value of that part of the Zoroastrian Law which teaches the means of purification.

IV (27-38 = Farg. VI, 6-9). The area of contagion of the Druj Nasu (the demon of corruption hidden within corpses) is greater or lesser depending on how high the virtue of the deceased places him in the scale of beings.

V (39-44). Purification of sacrificial instruments defiled by contact with the nasu.

12. A question that troubled theologians and frequently fed controversy. Water and fire are sacred; they are the work of Ahura, from whom only life comes, and yet they cause death, as if they came from Ahriman. "If a Zoroastrian lights a fire for a hundred years," said Saadi, "should he fall into it at the end, it will burn him":

If one lights fire for a hundred years, should he fall into it even for a moment, it will burn him.

Christians, in their polemics with Zoroastrian priests, mocked the ingratitude of fire: "Our hands," as Elisée has a mage say, "have grown hard and calloused from wielding the axe, our backs are bent under the weight of the wood, our eyes are red and constantly watering from the sharpness of the smoke that pours out. If we draw near to worship it, it burns us without the slightest regard; if we do not draw near, it reduces itself to ash" (trans. Garabed, p. 211).

The word astódán properly means an "ossuary": it appears, in the sense of "tomb," in a Greco-Aramaic inscription from Limyra in Lycia dating to the 4th or 5th century BCE, that is to say the last century of the Achaemenids: [a]stódanah zanah ... rtim bar Arzapi, "this is the tomb (τὸν τάφον) of [A]rtim[as], son of Arzapi." One can see from this passage that it was by no means absolutely forbidden to gather the remains of the dead, provided they were stripped of flesh. Appendix. — Medicine according to the Nask Hûspâram.

The greater part of this Fargard deals with the Druj Nasu and the purification of objects defiled by the nasu, that is to say by contact with death: clothing, wood, grain, earth, the Dakhmas, a woman who has given birth to a stillborn child, dishes, and the cow.

Section VII deals with an entirely different subject: the trials one must undergo in order to practice medicine, and the fees of the physician. We will find further on, at the end of the Vendidad, three Fargards devoted entirely to medicine, or rather to its mythical origins and the religious treatment of diseases (Farg. XX-XXII). The Yasht of Ardibahisht (Yt. III) is also, to a large extent, a medical Yasht. This is all that remains of the medical literature of the Avesta which Alexander, according to the Rivayats, had taken away and had translated into Greek. The Sassanid Avesta still contained other texts relating to medicine, and the most interesting one is preserved for us in the analysis of the Nasks: it formed part of the Nask Hûspâram, the 17th Nask, the 3rd of the legal Nasks. We consider it useful to reproduce in an appendix the analysis given of it by the Dinkart.

APPENDIX A

FUNERAL CEREMONIES AMONG THE PARSIS

We think it useful to summarize here the funeral ceremonies currently in use among the Parsis. We will point out as we go the ways in which they differ from ancient practice: the differences, here as in the ritual (vol. I, xci), arise chiefly from losses sustained in modern practice.
Funeral ceremonies are of two kinds: some dispose of the remains of the dead, while others act for the benefit of the soul.

I

The principle that governs the ceremonies of the first kind is the fear of contagion or, as the Avesta calls it, of the Druj Nasu, the Druj-Carrion. Death, once it has come, remains: visible proof of this is given by the corruption that quickly takes hold of the corpse and spreads infection around it: it was imagined in the form of a horrible fly,

All the ceremonies of this kind can be summed up in two words, the very same words that sum up today all prophylactic measures in cases of epidemic: 1° interrupt communications between the living and the real or supposed center of infection; 2° destroy that center itself.

As soon as the patient is evidently beyond saving, on one hand the shroud that is to clothe the corpse is washed, and the isolated funeral chamber³ that is to receive it while awaiting its transfer to the Dakhma is prepared; on the other hand two or more priests are summoned to recite for him the formula of Penitence, the Patet. If the dying person is able to recite it himself, whether alone or following the priests, his salvation is all the more assured. In the absence of the Patet, the Ashem vohû, recited at the last breath, suffices⁴. "Whoever recites the Patet, whatever sins he may have committed, will not go to hell; he will receive his punishment at the head of the Cinvat bridge, and then will be led to his place (in Paradise)⁵." An instant before death, a few drops of the Hôm prepared for the sacrifice are poured into the dying person's mouth, as a symbol of immortality and resurrection: this, it is known, is the white Haoma that will be the instrument of resurrection at the end of the world⁶.

The body of the dying person is then washed with water and dressed in cotton garments, white and absolutely clean⁷. One of the relatives ties the Kosti on him while reciting the Ahura Mazda Khudâi⁸, so that he may die wearing the livery of the Mazdean. He is then laid out on the ground on a white cotton sheet: two men sit at his side, and at the moment he dies the Ashem vohû is murmured in his ear.

There are two kinds of Nasâ-sâlârs: the Khândyas, simple bearers, whose entire function is to carry the corpse from the house to the gate of the Dakhma; and the Nasâ-sâlârs properly so called, who perform the washing of the dead and who alone have the right to enter the Dakhma. The former are merely the laborers of the funeral, while the latter have something of a religious character in their functions. The expression nashu-kasha in the Avesta seems to designate the Khândyas alone; the Nasâ-sâlâr is designated by the name Ratu, meaning "chief" (cf. p. 121, note 20).

The Nasâ-sâlârs, two in number 10, wash themselves, put on clean clothes, perform the Kosti, and take the bâj 11; then, performing the paivand — that is, holding on to one another by means of a piece of cloth linking them by the arm — they enter the room where the dead person is laid out. The two watchers then yield their place to the two Nasâ-sâlârs, who set about covering the body: the head alone remains uncovered. In some parts of Gujarat, the Padân is placed on the dead person 12. The body is then carried to a stone slab placed in a corner, and the arms are crossed over the chest 13.

In some parts of Gujarat, the method recommended in the Vendidad (VIII, 8) is still followed; that is, the body is placed on the ground, in a pit a few fingers deep, on a layer of sand 14. The task at hand is to expel it: this is the work of the Sag-did, the "Dog's Gaze." It was believed that a dog that looks upon a corpse drives out the demon lodged within it: the dog that howls at death and sees it pass undoubtedly possesses knowledge and powers that man does not. The most powerful dog against the Druj is the four-eyed dog (cathru-cashma), that is, one with two spots above its eyes, or the white dog with yellow ears 15. In the absence of these dogs, designated by their rare and unusual features for supernatural functions, one could resort to an ordinary dog (a sheepdog, a watchdog, a hunting dog, a stray dog) 16. The dog is brought near the dead person, and when it brings its muzzle close to the corpse, it drives away the Druj. The Sag-did is repeated at the beginning of each Gâh, for as long as the body remains in the house.

Once the Sag-did has been performed, fire is brought into the room and kept burning with fragrant woods, whose sweet-smelling flame kills the demons in every direction the wind carries it 17. A priest, seated at least three paces from the dead person, recites the Avesta until the moment the body is transferred to the Dakhma.

The transfer to the Dakhma takes place during the day, since the body must be exposed to the sun (Vd. V, 13; VI, 51). If death occurs at the beginning of the night, the transfer takes place the following morning; if it occurs late in the night or very early in the morning, the transfer takes place in the evening. In the case of accidental death, the delay is longer, since the Druj Nasu does not take immediate possession of the body — in other words, the decomposition of the body is slower 18.

They place the bier near the dead person and take the Bâj: then they recite in bâj: "According to the prescriptions of the creator Ahura Mazda, according to the prescriptions of the Amshaspands, according to the prescriptions of Adarbâd-Mahraspand, according to the prescriptions of the Dastûr of this time": then they sit in silence near the dead person. Here begins the recitation of the Gâthas; this is the spiritual struggle against the Druj, succeeding the material struggle.

Two priests, holding each other in paivand, at the door of the room or at least three paces from the dead person, recite the prayers of the Gâh, take the Bâj, then begin the recitation of the Gâtha Ahunavaiti (Hâs XXVIII-XXXIV). Upon reaching Hâ XXX, 4, at the words:

maibyô khshathrem aojônghvat yahyâ varedâ vanaêmâ Drujem

"to mine the mighty sovereignty, by the force of which we shall destroy the Druj,"

they stop; the Nasâ-sâlârs lift the body from the slab or the pit where it rests and place it on the iron bier. Then the priests, turning toward the bier, complete the Gâtha. Once the Gâtha is finished, a new Sag-dîd is performed: the relatives and friends who have gathered during this time come to take a last look at the deceased, before whom they bow — this is the Sejdo.

The Nasâ-sâlârs then leave the house and entrust the body to the Khândyas, who, also walking in pairs and in paivand, carry the bier with the corpse from the house to the gate of the Dakhma. The attendants follow the body at a distance to the end of the street: the relatives and intimates,

Their task completed, the Nasâ-sâlârs close the Tower behind them. The relatives, who had been waiting at some distance from the Tower, rise, finish the Bâj they had begun, release the paivand cord, and say: "We repent of all our sins. Homage to you! We worship the souls of the dead, the Fravashis of the righteous²⁷." Then they take some gômêz, wash their faces and the exposed parts of their bodies, perform the Kosti, recite the Patet inserting into it the name of the deceased who will benefit from it, return home, and take a bath.

During the three following days, a fire is kept burning near the place where the body had rested before being taken to the Dakhma. No one must occupy this place for nine days in winter, and for one month in summer²⁸. A lamp is burned there for nine days or one month depending on the season; nearby, a vase of water holds flowers that are renewed morning and evening.

During the first three days, the family abstains from meat²⁹ and eats only vegetables and fish³⁰. In former times it was even forbidden to cook any food in the house: relatives or friends would prepare food for the bereaved family and send it to them.

II

These first three days are those in which the soul of the deceased, still attached to the earth, remaining near the head of the dead person, experiences inexpressible joys or sufferings according to the life it has led³¹. During these three days of intermediate existence, which form what is called the sadis³², the soul, reduced to the weakness of birth, is in greater need than ever of the protection of the angels. The guardian angel of spirits is Srôsh, who is also charged with keeping the account of the good and evil deeds of the deceased³³. Thus all religious ceremonies celebrated during this period for the benefit of the soul of the dead are performed "for the satisfaction" (khshnûmainê) of Sraosha. The following are these ceremonies:

At the beginning of each Gâh, two priests or more, together with the relatives of the deceased, recite the Srôsh-bâj, the prayer of whichever Gâh one is in, and conclude with the Patet offered for the intention of the deceased.

At night, at the beginning of the Gâh Aiwisrûthrima, the Afrîngân is celebrated in honor of Srôsh with the ordinary ceremonies of the Afrîngâns³⁴. The Avestan portion of the Afrîngân consists of a Karda from the Srôsh Yasht, the 7th Karda (LVII, 15-18), dedicated to the praise of Sraosha as protector of the world and destroyer of the Druj and the demons. The Afrîngân Dahmân is recited³⁴.

In addition to these prayers and ceremonies celebrated at home, the Yasna, the Srôsh Darûn, and sometimes the Vendidad itself are recited at the nearby fire temple, in Khashnûman of Srôsh. We already know what the Yasna and the Vendidad are: the Srôsh Darûn or Bâj³⁵ is a partial Yasna, without Hôm, in which the darûn is the sole offering; it comprises the recitation of the Hâs

At the Gah Uzirin of the third day, relatives, friends, and priests gather: the prayers of the Gah are recited, along with the Srosh Hadhokht (Yt. XI) and the Patet. This ceremony is called in India the Uthumna. It is at the end of this ceremony that the relatives and friends of the deceased announce the charitable acts they are performing to commemorate his memory, or the charitable bequests he himself made in his will³⁷. If the deceased was a public benefactor, the entire Anjuman attends the ceremony and the chief priest or one of the notables proposes to the community that his name be recalled and blessed in public ceremonies. There are all sorts of degrees in this canonization, which may be local or universal, depending on whether the deceased's services were limited to a particular local community or extended to the entire Parsi community. The Farvardin Yasht presents the oldest list of these canonizations: it is not impossible that it contains modern additions and that recent historical names have been inserted into this list, which is dominated by legendary names or names that have become such through antiquity. The Afrin Rapithwin contains a list of Sassanid names. The Nirang boi dadan reaches back into the period of the emigration.

The dawn that follows fixes the definitive fate of the soul: it is the moment when it presents itself at the Cinvat bridge, where it will undergo the final judgment before Mithra, assisted by Rashnu, the Genius of Righteousness, and Arshtat, the Genius of Truth. From that point, a series of new ceremonies is held to assist the soul of the deceased before its judges: these are the ceremonies called the cihârum, or the fourth day. Beyond these special ceremonies celebrated on individual dates, there are general ceremonies for the dead, similar to those of All Saints' Day: these are the ceremonies of the Farvardijân, that is to say the last ten days of the year, a time when the souls of the dead descend once more to earth to receive the honors and prayers of their loved ones⁴².

When a corpse is laid there, the vultures, nature's scavengers, have within an hour or two completed their task, devouring the flesh and everything that decomposes 5. The dried skeletons are twice a year cast down into the central well, where the Nasâ-sâlârs have already, at each new deposit, thrown the clothing of the deceased, and under the action of rain, the atmosphere, and the tropical sun, everything is soon reduced to dust.

Holes dug inside the tower allow the water and rain 6, which have become infected by falling on the corpses, to drain into four underground channels: these channels lead to four underground wells whose floors are covered with a thick layer of sand, which acts as a filter: the channels are separated from the wells by pieces of charcoal and sandstone renewed from time to time. The polluted water thus undergoes a double filtration which renders it pure to the pure earth.

The various acts involved in the construction of a Dakhma are accompanied by religious ceremonies.

A few days later, the excavations complete, one proceeds to the laying out of the tower: this is the ceremony of the Tânâ, or of the thread. One begins by driving into the middle of the site an iron nail about a foot and a half long, which marks the center of the tower; one then drives in four nails positioned at the south-east, south-west, north-west, and north-east of the building⁷; then the four series of nine smaller nails⁸ placed between these four master nails, alternately on the outer circle and on an inner circle; then four series of sixty-five nails each, forming two parallel lines of thirty-two nails, which follow the direction of the drainage channel, the sixty-fifth nail facing the master nail m. The nails having been set, one winds the thread around the master nail of the south-east, then around each of the other master nails, until the thread returns to the starting point; after this quadrangular circuit, the thread goes around the building a second time, winding one by one around the thirty-six intermediate nails. Having returned a second time to the starting point, it winds around the sixty-five nails of column A, then around the sixty-five nails of column B, of column C, and finally of column D, where it stops. These threads, says Anquetil after a Rivayât, signify that the Dakhma is, so to speak, suspended in the air and does not touch the ground.

The building complete, one proceeds to the consecration. It lasts three days. The tower is surrounded by a pâvi, and two priests celebrate in the central well, each morning at the Hâvan Gâh, the Yasna, and each night at the Gâh Ushahin, the Vendidad; all in honor of Srôsh: on the fourth day in the morning the Yasna is celebrated in honor of Ormazd himself. Attached to each Dakhma is a chapel called a sâgri, where those present pray while the Nasâ-sâlârs carry the body into the Dakhma. It consists of two symmetrical halls. One is open, and there the Afrîngâns are recited; people come there especially on the days of Jashni — that is, the days that bear the name of the month and are days of festival and commemoration. The other hall is closed and contains the fire: on the side facing the tower, a lattice with oblique openings directs the eternal ray onto the dead, through a gap left in the parapet of the tower.

The Dakhmas are built far from the city⁹, in order to keep the dead as far as possible from the dwelling-place of the living. Once it is consecrated, only the Nasâ-sâlârs have the right to enter it¹⁰.

We do not know whether the form of the Dakhma in the time of the Vendidad was already that of the modern Dakhma¹¹. The Vendidad also authorized the use of astôdâns¹², that is, stone ossuaries, and in the absence of special constructions, it was sufficient to expose bodies on remote heights¹³.

We have already seen (p. 150) that before the laying out of the dead, two priests recite the Gâtha Ahunavaiti; this is what is called in India the Gâh sârnâ (Gâthâo srâvayêiti). Such is modern practice. The present Fargard proves that in ancient practice the five Gâthas and the Yasna Haptanhâiti were recited.
The text taken literally might suggest that these texts were not recited in their entirety, but only the stanzas of particular efficacy that are repeated two, three, or four times (the bishâmrûta, the thrishâmrûta, the cathrushâmrûta). Modern practice, which, though abbreviated according to its usual tendency and having reduced the recitation to the first Gâtha, nevertheless recites it in full — this makes it more than likely that the recitation was complete: the purpose of the Fargard is simply to identify the passages for which a single recitation does not suffice and which are moreover recited with a particular emphasis (framrava); it goes without saying that the rest is said once.
The indications of this Fargard are in perfect accord with the liturgical indications of the Yasna: it is a genuine specimen of that Zend ritual literature of which the Pahlavi Nirangistân has preserved for us several other examples (cf. vol. I, xcii-xciii, and below, Fragments).

FARGARD 12

This Fargard is absent from the ancient manuscripts with a Pahlavi translation: it is found only in the Vendidad Sadé¹. Moreover, the analysis of the Vendidad in the Dinkart likewise ignores this chapter, and since that analysis is based on the old Pahlavi translation², it seems natural to conclude either that this chapter did not originally belong to the Vendidad and was added after the composition of the Dinkart — since the author of the Dinkart did not find it in the Pahlavi Vendidad he was following — or that for some reason that escapes us no Pahlavi translation was made of it: in either case, the authenticity of the chapter would be called into question. But the analysis of the Dinkart is far from complete, and the omission of this chapter proves no more than the omission of Fargard X or Fargard XXI, about which the Dinkart likewise says nothing. Furthermore, the Pahlavi Vendidads, while omitting Fargard XII, assign the number XIII to the chapter that follows it, which suggests that their omission is a pure accident and that the manuscript from which ours derive had lost the corresponding leaves. The Avestan text itself, as given in the Vendidad Sadé, seems to preserve for us a direct trace of this old Pahlavi translation: there are three words foreign to the text whose presence in § 7 can only be explained by the hypothesis of a quotation introduced by the Pahlavi Commentary and which, as often happened, found its way from there into the Vendidad Sadé.

The prescriptions of the preceding chapters were of a general character and did not depend on the nature of the believer's relationship with the deceased: those of this chapter are specific to the relatives of the deceased and determine the relative length of the upaman, which varies according to the degree of kinship. The precise meaning of the word has not been established with certainty: upaman properly means "to remain, to wait"³. In what does the waiting consist in the present case? The second paragraph, if it forms a unit with the first, would lead one to believe that it concerns a temporary abandonment of the house by the relatives of the deceased: even today, in Persia, a son abandons the house where his father died; he would fear "the evil step," the bad qadim; a man's house must die with him⁴: he abandons it and goes to build elsewhere: it is for this reason that cities in Persia die and relocate so quickly. But this is a superstition too contrary to the utilitarian spirit of Zoroastrianism, and we have seen that the Vendidad expressly condemns the custom of the people of Herat of abandoning for a month the house where a man has just died (I, 9, and note 20). We therefore assume that the word upaman simply designates a period of mourning⁵ marked by abstention from ordinary activities. In current practice, there is, as far as I know, no formal mourning period, apart from that of the first three days: there is only the celebration of the Afringân in memory of the deceased on the 10th day after death (dahum), on the 30th day (sîrôz) and at the end of the year (sâlrôz).

The mourning period is doubled for relatives who died without confession, which suggests that this period was marked by particular prayers, especially no doubt by the recitation of the Patet for the benefit of the deceased. It is all the longer the closer the kinship. The maximum is for the father of the family or the mother of the family, who must not be confused with the father and mother: this refers to the head of the family, who, in
