FARGARD 14

This Fargard is the continuation and development of the last section of the preceding one: it deals with "the great crime of killing a water-dog and the details of the expiation" (madam girán vinásih-i zaktalúntan-i bavrak-i âpik; Dinkart, l. l., § 56).

The protected animal is called in Avestan udra upâpa, "the udra that lives in the waters," and it is linked to the family of the dog, since it is born from one (Farg. XIII, 51 ff.). Later texts call it sag-i âbi, "water-dog" (Saddar, LXXXVI), or bavrak-i âpik, "the water-bavrak" (Dinkart, v. s.; Minókhard, XXXVI, 10). The word bavrak represents the Avestan bawri, which appears elsewhere as the name of an aquatic animal (upâpô; Yt. V, 129), and the Bundahish (XIV, 19) formally identifies the bavrak-i âpik with the water-dog, which gives reason to believe that the udra and the bawri are one and the same animal.

The bawri has generally been identified with the beaver, for a purely philological reason, because the word phonetically represents the Latin fiber and the English beaver. But there is no beaver in Persia except along the Araxes (W. T. Blanford, Eastern Persia, Zoology, II, 51). The expression "water-dog," sag-i âbi, designates only the otter, and the very name udra seems to confirm this identification, since it is identical to the Germanic name of the animal, otter. Its other name, bawri, is doubtless connected to its color: for one cannot separate it from the Sanskrit babhru, meaning brown. The reasons that make the udra so sacred are not stated. The Bundahish says only: "The water-bavrak was created to fight against the demon who is

ZEND-AVESTA: VENDIDAD. — FARGARD 14 211

in the waters (bafrak-i dpig pun hamêst·irîh-i dévôk-i dar miâ yahvûnêt yahbûnt yakôyamûnêt). He doubtless understands by demon the harmful animals, or those reputed as such, that are found in water; perhaps the water-rats, ἐνύδρους μῦς, whose extermination the Magi, according to Plutarch (Quest. conviv., IV, 5, 2), regarded as a pious work.

The exorbitant penalties imposed against the killer of the udra give this entire chapter an air of extravagant fancy. One should doubtless see in this nothing more than one of those devices common to religious legislation, which, in order to ensure greater respect for a rule that cannot sufficiently defend itself on its own merits and that one might be tempted not to take seriously enough, deliberately inflate the scale of the threatened punishment. A crime that draws upon the one who commits it penalties so severe and so varied must be a terrible crime. Imagine in our own day a law protecting small birds and punishing violations with twenty years of hard labor and a fine of 100,000 francs, or better yet with eternal damnation.

FARGARD 17

1 (1-6). What must be done with hair that is cut.
I (7-10). What must be done with nails that are cut¹.

The cult of hair and nails, which is the subject of this Fargard, has, among certain peoples and at certain periods, combined with ideas relating to the resurrection. In Ireland, it is forbidden to burn hair; it must be buried: its owner will recover it at the resurrection². It is the same idea that made the martyrs so fearful of the punishment of fire and brought about the miracle of Saint Eulalia so many times³. The flamines were required to bury their nails and hair beneath a fruit tree⁴: in that case, at least, the resurrection is out of the question. The starting point of these precautions is probably in that impression, so keenly felt in Parsism, that everything separated from the body is dead and consequently becomes a seat of corruption and infection. Ideas of hygiene were therefore not foreign to these practices (§ 3).

The Kôsti (z. aiwyâonha, Évanghin) is the girdle that the Zoroastrian never removes, and which is at once the visible sign that he belongs to the Mazdean community and the bond that attaches him to it. The faithful person who wears the Kôsti participates in all the good works accomplished by his fellow believers (Saddar, ch. x). The Kôsti is a hollow, cylindrical girdle made of 72 braided strands of white wool and is wound three times around the waist: these three turns represent humat, hûkht, hvarsht — good thoughts, good words, good deeds. The 72 strands correspond to the 72 Hâs of the Yasna; they are braided into six thick cords of twelve each: these six cords represent the six Gâhânbârs, etc. (Edal Daru apud Wilson, The Parsi Religion, 163): it separates in man the upper region, which belongs to Ormazd, from the lower region, which belongs to Ahriman (Gujastak Abâlish). On the manner of tying the Kosti, see Khorda Avesta, Nirang kôsti.

The Sadéré is a sleeved shirt with a small pocket at the front of the collar, called giribân or kissai karfa, the pocket of good works. The faithful person, when putting on the Sadéré, must look at his giribân and ask himself whether it is filled with good works. — The Zend name of the Sadéré is unknown: M. Tahmuras has proposed the Zend vastrem, "the garment" (par excellence); however, the corruption would be too great. The Pahlavi names are shapîk and tashkûk.

On the Kôsti and the Sadéré, see Dastur Jamaspji M. J. Asana, A short treatise on the Navjot ceremony, Bombay, 1887.

in the morning he cries out to men: "How long will you keep sleeping?" (Grünbaum, ZDMG., XXXI, 210). — Cf. Mirkhond, Early Kings of Persia, tr. Shea, p. 57. It is also said that there is in heaven a rooster that sits beneath the throne of Allah, counts the hours of night and day, and when the hour of prayer arrives, intones the tesbih that all earthly roosters repeat.

25. Parôdarsh, translated pêsh-dakhshak, "the one who indicates first," that is to say "the one who announces the day." "He beats his wing, then utters a cry." darsh is the nominative of -dares (Sanskrit driç, which in Avestan means "to make visible").

26. Kahrkatâs, kark (Persian کرک). The name appears to be an onomatopoeia: it may perhaps be a corruption of the Vedic krikadàçu (Études iraniennes, II, 159): it would have been borrowed from India. — "When one does not call it by this name, it can act better"; cf. Farg. XIII, note 4.
